title: Contracts & Instruments
hook: MNQ isn't just a ticker on your screen. Know what you're actually trading.

launchpad.outcome: Name the common futures instruments and explain the difference between a mini and a micro contract.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If someone switches from 1 MNQ contract to 1 NQ contract, does their risk stay the same?

slides.body:
The instrument is the market. The contract count is your size inside that market.

MNQ, NQ, MGC, and ES are instruments — they tell you what market you're trading. 1, 2, or 5 contracts tells you how much exposure you have to that instrument's move. Same market. Very different dollar and emotional weight.

check.prompt: A trader moves from MNQ to NQ but keeps the same number of contracts because "the chart looks the same."

options.label: That's a mistake
options.body: The contract multiplier is different, so the same price move produces very different P&L and risk.
options.why: Exactly — the chart shape being similar doesn't mean the dollar exposure is similar.

options.label: That's fine
options.body: NQ and MNQ are the same size, just different tickers.
options.feedback: They're not the same size — MNQ is 1/10 the contract multiplier of NQ.

slides.kicker: Meet the instruments with the real numbers
slides.title: Meet the instruments with the real numbers
slides.body: Tap an instrument to see the exact dollar amount attached to one point and one tick. Then check the table below — this is where it starts feeling real.

instruments.label: MNQ
instruments.tone: Lighter Nasdaq exposure — great for learning.

instruments.label: NQ
instruments.tone: This hits 10x harder than MNQ per point.

instruments.label: ES
instruments.tone: Very heavy point value — not casual.

slides.body:
Think of it simply: the instrument is the vehicle, and contract count is how many of that vehicle you're driving.

If price moves 10 points on MNQ, one contract gives you $20. That same 10-point move on NQ gives you $200 — ten times the weight, same chart shape.

Same chart logic. Very different dollar consequence. This is why size and instrument selection matter just as much as the setup.

slides.quote: A lot of people don't have a strategy problem first. They have a size problem first. They're trying to learn on instruments that hit too hard for where they are mentally.

slides.title: Contracts lab — see the dollars attached
slides.body: Pick the instrument. Pick the points. Pick the contract count. Watch how fast the number — and the way it feels — changes.

slides.title: Contract vs. instrument
slides.body: Beginners blur these together all the time. We're not doing that here.

options.label: Better understanding
options.body: MNQ is the instrument. If I take 3 MNQ contracts, the market is still MNQ — what changed is my size.
options.feedback: Exactly. The instrument is the market. The contract count is your size inside that market. Those are connected, but not interchangeable.

options.label: Bad understanding
options.body: A contract and an instrument are basically the same thing, so I don't need to separate them.
options.feedback: Not this one — when you mix those up, you stop respecting the actual dollar weight attached to what you chose.

quickCheck.prompt: If you go from 1 NQ contract to 2 NQ contracts, what changed?

options.label: Your size changed, not the instrument
options.why: Exactly. It's still NQ — what changed is your size and the dollar weight of the move.

options.label: The instrument changed
options.feedback: Not quite. NQ stayed NQ — you just increased how much NQ exposure you took.

options.label: Nothing really changed
options.feedback: No — the dollar amount attached to the move absolutely changed.

slides.title: Build the idea
slides.body: Let's make sure this is really clicking.

steps.prompt: A newer trader wants Nasdaq exposure with smaller dollar weight. Best fit?
What helps someone stay more teachable while still learning?

slides.goodFeedback: Clean logic. MNQ gives Nasdaq exposure with lighter point value, and a smaller contract count keeps a trader more teachable while she's still learning.
slides.badFeedback: Almost. The deeper point here is choosing a lighter instrument or lighter size when you're still learning to read the market.

items.label: The instrument is the market.
items.desc: MNQ, NQ, MGC, ES tell you what you're trading.

items.label: The contract count is your size.
items.desc: 1 contract and 5 contracts of the same instrument are not emotionally the same trade.

items.label: Dollar amounts attach fast.
items.desc: One point means something very different on MNQ than it does on ES or NQ.

items.label: Micros keep you teachable.
items.desc: Smaller exposure gives you room to actually learn before your emotions hijack the lesson.

slides.prompt: Imagine another AGHF girl asks: "What's actually different between MNQ and NQ?" How would you explain it to her?
slides.modelAnswer: They're the same underlying market — the Nasdaq-100 — just different contract sizes. MNQ is the micro version, worth 1/10 of what NQ is per point. So the exact same price move means very different dollar risk depending on which one you're trading.

takeaways: The instrument is the market — the contract count is your size inside it.
Micro contracts (MNQ, MES, MGC) are a fraction of their mini counterparts (NQ, ES, GC).
Dollar amounts attach fast — the same move means very different money depending on the instrument and size.
remember: Know the instrument. Know its value. Know your risk.
